newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African money mkt shortage at record high.
newsitem.headline: S.African money mkt shortage at record high.

text.p: South Africa's money market shortage moved to a record high at the weekend, maintaining the stranglehold on liquidity in place since the beginning of this year.
The Reserve Bank indicated the shortage at a record 11.680 billion rand on Saturday, slightly up from 11.645 billion rand on Friday.

The Reserve Bank's money and capital market assistant general manager Roelf du Plooy said the reason for the continued high shortage was the fact that commercial banks were assuming the central bank's role of providing forward cover to South African businesses, a factor pointed to by deputy governor James Cross last week.
"Most of it is due to foreign exchange flows at the moment," Du Plooy said.

"The reason for that is that the banks are taking over from the Reserve Bank the role of providing forward cover ... and due to that they have to carry larger volumes of foreign exchange on their books which they are not selling back to the Reserve Bank," he said.
Du Plooy also pointed to the high amount of notes and coins in circulation -- currently 19.65 billion rand.

"We saw an outflow back into the economy so there were less deposits at the banks and the shortage increased a bit," he said. "That is a normal thing that happens at month-end...and over the last few days we have seen it swinging back," he said.

Du Plooy expected the shortage to remain high at least until the end of this week. "As long as banks keep more dollars on their portfolios we can expect the shortage to remain high. I don't see an immediate reduction in the shortage in the short-term," he said.
Money market traders said the high shortage had had little impact on short-term rates as the market was well aware that it was the Reserve Bank's intention to keep a tight grip on liquidity.

"What they (Reserve Bank) have been doing is manipulating the shortage by taking money out of the Tax and Loan accounts and putting it into the exchequer accounts. (Bank Governor Chris) Stals has repeatedly said that he want to keep the short-end of the market tight so this could just be part of their policy," one trader said.

"(Saturday's shortage of) 11.68 bln rand is a bad number but on the other side of the coin it has not really affected our money market like it normally would because people know it is being manipulated," he said.
Three-month deposit rates were quoted steady at between 16.50 and 16.55 percent bid, while the 90-day BA rate was also unmoved at between 15.90 and 16.10 percent.

Another senior trader noted, however, that the high shortage did not necessarily imply that short-term rates should rise. It was rather an indication of the central bank's current monetary policy stance.
"We have a tight monetary policy at the moment which is ensuring that rates stay where they are, but are we saying that monetary policy is so tight that rates must go higher?" he said
"I don't believe that is what (the Reserve Bank) is trying to achieve. The message is that monetary policy is tight, it has not been relaxed and we are not about to relax it."
